stimulus.text: The third page of the engrossed Constitution, signed at Philadelphia on September 17, 1787, carries the end of Article II and the start of Article III. It says the person with the most electoral votes shall be President “if such Number be a Majority of the whole Number of Electors appointed,” and that if no person has a majority, “the House of Representatives shall in like Manner chuse the President” from the five highest on the list. Section 2 names the president “Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States” and gives power, “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties” and to appoint ambassadors and “Judges of the supreme Court.” Article III, Section 1 vests judicial power in “one supreme Court,” and says judges “shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour” and that their pay “shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office.”

stem: According to the page, what happens if no candidate for president wins a majority of the electoral votes?

options.text: The Senate chooses the president from the two highest vote-getters.
options.misconception: The page gives the choice to the House, not the Senate, and from five names, not two.

options.text: The candidate with the most votes becomes president without a majority.
options.misconception: The page requires a majority; without one, the House chooses.

options.text: A new election is held with the same electors voting again.
options.misconception: The page says the House chooses, not that the electors vote again.

options.text: The House chooses the president from the five highest on the list.

rationales.D: The page says that if no person has a majority, the House shall choose the president “from the five highest on the List.”
rationales.A: The page gives this choice to the House of Representatives, not the Senate.
rationales.B: The page requires a majority of electors; the most votes alone are not enough.
rationales.C: The page sends the choice to the House, not back to the electors.
rationales.general:
1. The page sets the rule for choosing a president: the most votes, if that number is a majority of electors.
2. It then covers the case where no person has a majority.
3. In that case the House of Representatives chooses, from the five highest on the list.
4. The Senate gets no role in this choice, and no new election is held.
Remember: when the electors fail to pick a winner, the Constitution sends the choice to the House.
